claims.text: Conventionally homogenized refractory high-entropy alloys have relatively coarse grains.
Conventionally homogenized refractory high-entropy alloys have uneven or irregular precipitate distributions.
The proposed treatment uses approximately 50% cold-rolling thickness reduction followed by short-time annealing slightly above the recrystallization threshold.
Cold rolling introduces a high density of dislocations.
The two-stage treatment will produce fine, uniformly recrystallized grains.
The two-stage treatment will promote a uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates.
Rolling-induced dislocations serve as nucleation sites for recrystallization during annealing.
Controlled short-time annealing near the recrystallization regime induces nanoscale precipitation.
Refined grains increase yield strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
Uniform nanoscale precipitates increase yield strength through precipitation strengthening.
Fine grains and uniformly distributed precipitates maintain or improve ductility by providing multiple well-distributed slip paths without overly impeding dislocation mobility.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength than an identical alloy processed by conventional homogenization.
The treated alloy will have greater ductility and work-hardening capacity than an identical alloy processed by conventional homogenization.
A controlled atmosphere is needed to avoid oxidation during the treatment.
Annealing far from the recrystallization regime or using substantially different rolling reductions may fail to produce the favorable microstructure.
Excessive grain growth can be avoided by optimizing rolling reduction and annealing temperature and time for the specific alloy.
